name: Amazon DynamoDB
oneLiner: Serverless key-value and document NoSQL with single-digit-millisecond latency.
whatItIs: DynamoDB is AWS's fully-managed NoSQL database, built for predictable low latency at any scale. You store items (JSON-like documents) in tables and fetch them by key in single-digit milliseconds, whether the table has a thousand rows or a trillion. It's serverless — no servers to size, automatic scaling, replication baked in — which makes it the default operational datastore for high-traffic AWS applications: user sessions, shopping carts, game state, IoT device records. It is not for analytics; it's for fast, reliable reads and writes of known keys at massive scale.

inPractice.narrative: A high-traffic app stores each user's cart and profile in DynamoDB, keyed by user ID, so reads/writes stay a few milliseconds even at peak. For analytics, the team doesn't query DynamoDB directly — they stream changes via DynamoDB Streams (or export to S3) into the data lake, where Athena/Redshift analyse them. So DynamoDB is the fast operational store up front, feeding the analytical world downstream rather than being queried by it.

coreConcepts.detail: Items are addressed by a partition key (which distributes data) and optional sort key (ordering within a partition). Good key design is everything — it determines performance and avoids hot partitions.
Managed partitioning spreads data/traffic so latency stays flat as the table grows — the core promise. DAX adds an in-memory cache for microsecond reads.
On-Demand (pay per request, auto-scales, no planning) or Provisioned (set read/write capacity units, cheaper for steady predictable load, with auto-scaling).
Global (GSI) and Local (LSI) secondary indexes allow queries on non-primary attributes — but you design them up front around access patterns.
DynamoDB Streams emit item-level changes, enabling event-driven processing, replication and feeding analytics/lakes.
A NoSQL modelling approach where multiple entity types share one table, shaped entirely around known access patterns rather than normalised relations.

whenToUse: High-traffic operational apps needing fast key-based reads/writes.
Predictable low latency at massive, spiky or unpredictable scale.
Serverless applications wanting a zero-ops, auto-scaling datastore.
Session stores, carts, user profiles, game/IoT state, leaderboards.
whenNotToUse: Ad-hoc analytical queries, aggregations and joins — use a warehouse/lake.
Access patterns you can't predict up front — relational flexibility fits better.
Complex multi-table joins and rich querying — that's a SQL database's job.
Large scans/reporting over the whole dataset — export to S3 and query there instead.

keyFacts.label: Global
keyFacts.value: Global Tables for multi-region active-active replication.

pricingShape: Two models. On-Demand bills per read/write request plus storage — no capacity planning, scales to zero-ish when idle, ideal for spiky/unknown traffic but pricier per request. Provisioned bills for the read/write capacity units you reserve (with auto-scaling), cheaper for steady, predictable load if sized well. Storage is per GB-month. Extras — GSIs (which consume their own capacity), Streams, DAX, Global Tables and backups — add cost. The big levers are capacity mode choice, efficient key design (to avoid wasted throughput), and not over-indexing.
gotchas: Poor partition-key design creates hot partitions that throttle despite plenty of provisioned capacity.
You must model around access patterns up front — DynamoDB punishes 'query it however later' thinking.
It's not for analytics; scanning the table for reports is slow and expensive — export to S3 instead.
Each GSI consumes its own throughput and storage; over-indexing multiplies cost.
On-Demand is convenient but can cost far more than well-sized Provisioned for steady workloads — pick deliberately.

equivalents.name: Bigtable
equivalents.note: Wide-column NoSQL for huge scale; Firestore is closer for document/serverless use.

equivalents.name: Azure Cosmos DB
equivalents.note: Multi-model, globally-distributed NoSQL; broader API surface than DynamoDB.
